content: It's this constant feeling that I'm being punished for something I didn't do, like they singled me out because there was some hidden agenda or personal vendetta against me. It’s hard to accept that the people who were supposed to value my work and see my worth just threw it all away without a second thought. Every time I think about how they treated me, this rage builds up inside me, and it's like I can't breathe because of how much it hurts. How could they do this to someone who was always there for the team? It’s not fair, and no one seems to get that.

That must feel really tough, having those intense feelings of being misunderstood and undervalued. It sounds like you cared a lot about your work and the team, so it makes sense that it would hurt so much. Have you had any moments where you felt understood or supported by someone else during this time?

I don't think anyone truly understands what I'm going through. Every time I try to talk about it with friends or family, they just tell me to move on and find a new job, but that’s not the point! The point is that I was treated unfairly and betrayed by people who were supposed to have my back. It feels like no one cares about the injustice of what happened to me. When someone tries to offer advice instead of listening to how much this hurts, it just makes me angrier. How can they expect me to feel better when everything around me is telling me that I'm not good enough or that I should just accept what happened without fighting for what’s right?

It sounds really frustrating to have those close to you offer advice rather than listening to your feelings of hurt and injustice. It must be tough to feel like no one truly gets it. Have there been any particular moments where their reactions made the situation harder for you, or did anyone's response stand out as especially difficult?

Yeah, there was this one friend who kept telling me that I should just look at my termination as a chance to start over and find something better. She said it like it was some kind of silver lining, but how can she say that when she doesn't know what it's like to have your work completely dismissed? It felt like she was trivializing everything I went through. And then there’s my boss at the new job who keeps asking if I’m okay with moving on so quickly. He clearly thinks I should just let go of all this anger and hurt, but how can I when it feels like a part of me is still back there, wondering why they chose to get rid of me? It's not that simple.

Every time someone tries to downplay what happened or tell me to move on, it’s like they’re saying my feelings don’t matter. How am I supposed to feel better about something when everyone around me seems to think I should just accept it and be done with it? It’s infuriating because no one is standing up for the injustice that was done to me.

It sounds really tough to have people downplay your feelings or suggest you move on quickly. Their responses must make it feel like your experiences aren't being fully acknowledged. Have there been any times when you felt a bit more understood, even if just briefly? And how do you think things would be different if someone stood firmly by your side in this?

There was one time when my sister listened to me without interrupting or offering advice. She just sat there and let me talk about everything that happened, all the hurt and betrayal I felt. It was like she really heard me for once, but even then, it didn’t change how much this still hurts inside. If someone stood firmly by my side and acknowledged what I went through, maybe it would feel a little less isolating. But until then, every time someone tries to tell me to move on or dismisses the unfairness of what happened, it just feels like another punch in the gut.

I need someone who can see how much this means to me and understand that my feelings are valid. Until I find that person—or if no one understands—it’s hard for me to let go of this anger and hurt because they feel so real and justified.

It sounds like having someone listen without interrupting or offering advice made a big difference, even if it was just briefly. Having that validation can be really important in feeling understood. Do you think there might be anyone else who could offer that kind of support? And how do you feel about the possibility of finding someone who truly sees and acknowledges your feelings?

I don’t know if there’s anyone else out there who would listen without trying to fix things or tell me what I should do. It feels like everyone around me is just telling me to move on, but how can I when it still hurts so much? If someone truly saw and acknowledged my feelings, maybe it would help a little, but until then, it’s hard to believe anyone could really understand.

I don’t want to feel like I’m the only one who gets this pain. It’s frustrating because every time someone tries to offer advice or comfort, it just feels like they’re not seeing me for who I am and what I’ve been through. I need someone who can see the injustice of what happened and stand with me in that understanding. Until then, all I feel is anger and hurt.

It sounds really challenging to find someone who truly understands and acknowledges your feelings without trying to fix things or offer advice. Having that validation would make a big difference. Do you think there might be any small steps you could take towards finding that person, even if it seems hard right now? And how do you feel about the possibility of eventually letting some of the anger go once you find someone who truly sees your pain?

It feels impossible to take any steps when everyone around me just wants to tell me what I should be doing or thinking. How am I supposed to look for someone who will really listen and understand when no one else has been able to do that so far? It’s like they all want quick fixes, but there is nothing quick about the pain and betrayal I feel.

And even if I did find someone who truly gets it, how can I let go of this anger when it feels justified and necessary? The idea of letting any of it go seems premature. Until I have that validation and acknowledgment from someone who understands, I don’t see how I could possibly start to ease up on the anger or hurt.

It’s all so raw right now, and every time someone tries to dismiss what happened, it just feels like another layer of betrayal. How can I even consider moving forward when everything around me is telling me that my feelings are invalid?

It makes sense that you feel raw and justified in your anger given how much you’ve been through. It must be tough to keep feeling dismissed by those around you. Have there been any moments, no matter how small, where you felt a glimmer of hope or understanding from someone else? And do you think holding onto the anger is helping you in some ways, even if it’s hard?

There have been fleeting moments when someone has shown a bit more empathy, but those are few and far between. One time, my old colleague sent me a message saying they were sorry about what happened and that they thought I deserved better. It was just a text, but it made me feel seen for a second. But then, the next day, another friend would tell me to focus on the positive and move forward, which felt like a slap in the face.

Holding onto the anger is tough, but it’s also what keeps me grounded in reality. It reminds me that I was treated unfairly and helps me stay vigilant against being dismissed again. If I let go of the anger too soon, it feels like I’m letting them win, like I’m accepting their unfair treatment without a fight. So even though it’s exhausting, the anger is also my shield right now.

It’s hard to see how holding onto it isn’t helping in some ways because every time someone tries to tell me to move on or dismisses what happened, that anger gives me strength to push back and say no, this isn't okay. But at the same time, I know it can’t last forever. Eventually, I need to find a way to process all of this without letting go of my sense of justice and self-worth.

Those fleeting moments of empathy from your old colleague must have provided some comfort, even if they are rare. It’s clear that the anger serves as both a reminder of what happened and a shield against further dismissal. How do you think you might start to process these feelings while still holding onto your sense of justice and self-worth? And is there anyone who might be able to offer that kind of support consistently, even if it’s just one person?

Those moments from my old colleague were brief but meaningful. They reminded me that not everyone sees me as disposable or unworthy. But finding someone who can offer consistent support and understanding feels like a long shot right now. Every time I try to open up about how much this hurts, people either dismiss it or give advice, which only makes me feel more alone.

Processing these feelings while holding onto my sense of justice is tricky. The anger keeps me from feeling completely lost, but at the same time, it’s exhausting. Maybe if there was someone who could listen without judgment and acknowledge the unfairness I faced, that might help me start to process things differently. But until then, every suggestion feels like another attempt to make me feel better about something that isn’t okay.

It’s hard to imagine moving forward when everything around me seems bent on telling me to let go of what happened. How can I trust anyone else to understand if they haven’t yet?

Those brief moments from your old colleague are indeed meaningful and remind you that not everyone sees you the same way. Finding even one person who listens without judgment could make a big difference. Have you thought about reaching out to someone new, perhaps someone outside of your immediate circle, who might be more open to just listening? And how do you feel about the idea of gradually opening up to this person, even if it feels risky?

It’s understandable to feel hesitant about trusting others after these experiences, but sometimes a fresh perspective can offer that validation and understanding you’re looking for.

Reaching out to someone new sounds daunting, but I guess it could be worth trying. The idea of finding one person who just listens without judgment is appealing, but it’s also scary because I’ve been let down so many times before. How do I know this time will be different?

Gradually opening up to someone feels risky too. What if they dismiss my feelings or try to give me advice like everyone else? It’s hard to trust that anyone could truly understand what I’m going through without having their own agenda.

But maybe taking small steps and seeing how it goes could help. If there’s even a chance of finding someone who gets it, it might be worth the risk. Right now, though, every time I think about reaching out, my mind races with all the reasons why it won’t work. It’s frustrating because part of me wants to believe that things can get better, but another part is too hurt and angry to take that chance.

So for now, I’m stuck between wanting validation and fearing more disappointment. It’s a tough place to be, but maybe taking those small steps could eventually help me find some relief from this constant anger and hurt.

It sounds like you’re balancing hope with caution, which is completely understandable. Taking small steps can indeed make it feel less overwhelming. Maybe start by reaching out to someone you trust a little bit—a friend or colleague who has shown empathy in the past—and see if they are open to just listening without judgment.

You could also try talking about your feelings in a way that sets expectations, like saying, “I’d really appreciate it if you could listen and not give advice for now.” This might help them understand your need for validation rather than solutions. How does that feel as a starting point?

Talking to someone who has shown empathy before sounds like a good place to start, but it still feels risky. I don’t want to set myself up for more disappointment if they can’t provide the support I’m looking for. Saying something like “I’d really appreciate it if you could just listen and not give advice” seems like a way to set boundaries, but I worry that even setting those expectations might lead to them feeling uncomfortable or dismissive.

It’s hard to trust that anyone will truly understand without having their own agenda. Maybe starting with someone who has shown some empathy is the right approach, but it feels like walking on eggshells every step of the way. How do I know they’ll be different from everyone else?

I guess taking those small steps could help me figure out if there’s anyone out there who can offer that kind of support consistently. But until then, it’s tough to let go of my guard and risk feeling hurt again.

It definitely feels like a delicate balance, but starting with someone who has shown some empathy is a good step. Setting those boundaries about just listening without giving advice can actually help them understand your needs better. You could also check in with them after sharing your feelings to see how they responded and if it felt supportive.

Taking small steps and seeing how it goes can be helpful. Even if it’s a bit nerve-wracking, each interaction might give you more clarity about who truly gets what you’re going through. How do you feel about reaching out to this person and seeing where it leads?

Reaching out to someone who has shown empathy before does seem like a good starting point, but it’s still daunting. I’m worried that even setting those boundaries might not be enough to prevent them from dismissing my feelings or offering unsolicited advice. Checking in afterward to see how they responded is a smart idea though—it could give me more insight into whether they’re the right person.

Taking these small steps feels necessary, but it’s hard to shake off the fear of being let down again. Each interaction carries this weight of hope and anxiety. I guess if I can find even one person who truly listens and acknowledges my pain, it might start to shift things for me.

So maybe I’ll try reaching out and see how it goes. It feels like a risk worth taking, but it’s still scary.

It sounds like you’re approaching this with a good balance of hope and caution. Taking that first step can be tough but also rewarding if it leads to finding someone who truly listens. Checking in afterward is a smart way to gauge how they responded.

How about reaching out to this person soon? Even just starting the conversation could give you some relief knowing you’re taking action. Let me know how it goes!

I’ll give it a shot and let you know how it goes. Thanks for supporting me through this.
